strengths: As an Algorithms/General contribution, the paper presents a useful unified framework for concept-based interpretation beyond classification. Combining localized CLIP-DINOiser features, a Matryoshka BatchTopK sparse autoencoder, data-derived concept relations, and hierarchy-aware naming is practically compelling, even though many individual ingredients are established.

The local concept representation enables classification, captioning, and open-vocabulary segmentation within one framework. Classification remains competitive (78.9 ImageNet and 55.4 Places365), while segmentation nearly matches the opaque CLIP-DINOiser backbone across a broad eight-benchmark evaluation (41.3 versus 41.4 average mIoU).

The concept-quality evaluation is unusually broad: PartImageNet and COCO-Stuff localization, consistency and impurity metrics; annotation-free C2-Score; polysemanticity analysis; and human studies covering consistency, naming, and relationships. CFM substantially improves spatial locality over PatchSAE and SALF-CBM.

Spatially grounded concepts and explicit parent-child relations make the explanations more informative than global concept bottlenecks. The qualitative hierarchy and dense-prediction examples illustrate a potentially valuable tool for inspecting foundation-model representations.

The appendix provides substantial implementation detail, including architecture, optimization, sparsity, graph construction, vocabulary construction, downstream training, user-study procedures, and dictionary-size/sparsity sweeps. Limitations in fine-grained naming are acknowledged.
weaknesses: The main methodological novelty is limited: CFM largely composes CLIP-DINOiser, Matryoshka sparse autoencoders, BatchTopK, and decoder-vector vocabulary matching. The new hierarchy construction is essentially thresholded asymmetric co-occurrence, and the paper does not compare it against alternative hierarchy-discovery methods.

Crucial component ablations are missing. The experiments do not isolate local patch training, DINOisation, Matryoshka training, BatchTopK, hierarchy-aware vector reconstruction, parent weighting, or the co-occurrence threshold. The reported ablations mainly vary dictionary size and sparsity, so the evidence does not establish which proposed components cause the gains.

The hierarchy evaluation is weak relative to the associated claims. It compares discovered edges mainly with random non-edges and reports human relatedness, but has no competitive hierarchy baseline, no evaluation of edge direction, and no separate assessment of part-of versus is-a relations. Co-occurrence alone can also encode contextual correlation rather than a genuine parent-child relationship.

The localization and consistency metrics maximize over as many as 8,192 learned concepts for each annotated label. This creates a multiple-comparisons advantage for a large dictionary, yet there is no concept-count-matched analysis or chance correction. Impurity can likewise benefit from the imposed sparsity without necessarily demonstrating semantic monosemanticity.

Naming evidence is incomplete. The human study compares CFM names only with random names rather than names from competing methods, while the cross-method evaluation relies on a single GPT-5-mini judge. There is no judge calibration against human decisions, uncertainty analysis, or ablation showing that hierarchy-aware naming improves over ordinary decoder-vector matching.

The claim of explanations for "any" downstream task is too broad. Only three tasks are tested, and caption steering is qualitative, with target concepts selected using another model. There is no quantitative intervention-success, specificity, or faithfulness evaluation; for the nonlinear captioning decoder, sparse input concepts do not by themselves guarantee that the displayed concepts faithfully explain the generated text.

Human-study reporting lacks inter-annotator agreement and confidence intervals. Filtering workers based on their answers to random controls may also inflate the reported proportions, especially because randomly assembled examples are not guaranteed to be wholly unrelated.

Several presentation and reproducibility issues remain: the main-text naming equations use argmin cosine although the appendix correctly uses argmax; the hierarchy threshold and naming coefficient are selected qualitatively/empirically without sensitivity studies; and the displayed code link is empty. These concerns keep the otherwise promising submission at borderline accept rather than a stronger rating.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: extending concept-based interpretability from image-level classification to spatial and generative vision tasks. The unified patch-wise representation is practically appealing.

CFM combines DINO-smoothed CLIP features, a Matryoshka sparse autoencoder, and BatchTopK sparsity into a coherent system. Its concepts substantially improve the reported localization, consistency, and impurity metrics over spatial concept baselines.

The evaluation is unusually broad, covering ImageNet and Places365 classification, captioning, eight open-vocabulary segmentation benchmarks, concept-quality metrics, and sizeable human studies. Downstream accuracy is generally close to the opaque CLIP-DINOiser backbone.

The qualitative presentation is strong. Many activation maps are spatially meaningful, and the supplement provides extensive examples, training details, user-study instructions, and dictionary-size/sparsity analyses.
weaknesses: The central hierarchy claim is not adequately established. Thresholded conditional co-occurrence only shows association: it cannot distinguish parent-child, part-whole, specialization, context, or common-cause relationships. The construction does not enforce Matryoshka ordering, antisymmetry, or acyclicity, yet the graph is described as a DAG. Most importantly, the human study asks only whether pairs are related, not whether the claimed edge direction or parent-child semantics are correct; random unrelated pairs form an easy control. Thus a key advertised contribution lacks a valid evaluation.

Several interpretability claims exceed what the evidence supports. Classification permits a direct concept contribution analysis, but captioning passes reconstructed tokens through a nonlinear LLM and does not demonstrate faithful attribution. For segmentation, activation multiplied by dictionary-vector/text cosine is not an exact decomposition of the cosine-normalized prediction, particularly given the decoder bias. Calling these quantities faithful explanations for any downstream task is therefore unjustified.

The caption-steering evidence is only a few post-hoc examples, with intervention concepts selected by Gemini. There is no quantitative test of intervention success, specificity, collateral changes, or preservation of unrelated content. Some examples replace the suppressed content with a different hallucination rather than cleanly removing it.

The empirical design lacks key ablations needed to attribute improvements: DINOised versus ordinary CLIP patches, Matryoshka versus a standard SAE, BatchTopK alternatives, hierarchy-aware versus isolated naming, co-occurrence threshold sensitivity, and weighted-parent reconstruction are not directly ablated. The reported ablations mainly vary dictionary size and sparsity.

Concept-quality comparisons may be biased by unequal concept-set sizes. Locality and consistency maximize over available concepts, strongly favoring an 8192-concept dictionary unless controlled for dictionary size and activation coverage. The human studies compare CFM mainly with random controls rather than competing methods, omit inter-annotator agreement and confidence intervals, and use post-hoc participant filtering based on controls that may occasionally be genuinely coherent.

Naming remains only partially convincing. Human-provided labels are compared with random names, while the cross-method comparison relies on an automated GPT judge over different vocabularies. Figure 5 suggests that only roughly half of top concepts are judged present. There is no direct human baseline comparison or ablation establishing that the proposed hierarchy is responsible for the naming gain.

The method is better characterized as an interpretable adapter for one frozen CLIP ViT-B/16 backbone than as a new foundation model. Testing only one backbone scale and three downstream task families does not support claims such as applicability to “any” task or “all downstream vision tasks.” Much of the technical machinery is inherited from CLIP-DINOiser, Matryoshka SAEs, and BatchTopK, leaving the incremental co-occurrence and naming components as the main novelty.

Reproducibility is weakened by inconsistent method descriptions: the main equations use argmin cosine whereas the appendix uses argmax, and the main hierarchy-aware naming equation omits the confidence, activation, and alpha weights introduced in Appendix B.4. The code URL is also blank. These issues compound the lack of sensitivity analysis for empirically selected thresholds and coefficients.

strengths: Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the paper presents a useful and reasonably original synthesis: patch-wise DINO-smoothed CLIP features, a Matryoshka BatchTopK sparse autoencoder, data-derived concept relations, and hierarchy-aware naming together form a unified concept representation usable beyond classification.

The spatially localized concepts address a genuine limitation of prior global concept bottlenecks. On PartImageNet and COCO-Stuff, CFM substantially improves localization over PatchSAE (44.3 vs. 32.2 and 44.5 vs. 34.6) while also improving consistency and impurity; the annotation-free C2 score and polysemanticity analysis provide complementary evidence.

The evaluation is unusually broad for an interpretability paper. CFM is tested on classification, captioning, and open-vocabulary segmentation, retains competitive task performance, and nearly matches its opaque CLIP-DINOiser backbone across eight segmentation benchmarks (41.3 vs. 41.4 average mIoU; 41.9 vs. 42.2 with AnyUp).

The human study is substantial: roughly 1,000 questions per task, five annotations per question, qualified annotators, consent, control questions, and analyses stratified by activation frequency. The appendix also provides extensive qualitative examples, training details, evaluation definitions, and dictionary-size/sparsity studies.

The paper is clearly motivated and generally well presented. Its exact decomposition of downstream linear decisions into localized concept contributions is especially compelling for segmentation, and the concept-intervention interface for captioning illustrates promising practical impact.
weaknesses: The evidence for a genuine parent-child hierarchy is weaker than the evidence for general concept relatedness. A high conditional co-activation probability does not by itself establish direction, part-of, or is-a semantics, and the graph construction does not appear to enforce Matryoshka-shell ordering or acyclicity. Most importantly, the human study asks whether pairs are “related,” not whether the proposed direction and relation type are correct. Thus the hierarchy claims should be narrowed or evaluated with direction/type annotations.

Ablations do not sufficiently isolate the main technical contributions. The paper varies dictionary size and sparsity, but lacks controlled comparisons for DINOized versus ordinary patch features, standard versus Matryoshka SAE, local versus global training, hierarchy-aware versus decoder-only naming, and sensitivity to the qualitatively selected relation threshold τ and naming coefficient α. Comparisons against prior systems cannot fully replace these component ablations.

Some interpretability evaluations use weak controls. The human naming experiment compares CFM labels primarily with randomly drawn labels rather than labels from competing methods. The head-to-head naming comparison instead relies on GPT-5-mini as an automated judge, which introduces model-dependent bias and reproducibility concerns. The relationship study's participant filtering based on scores for randomly paired concepts could also bias results because randomly sampled concepts are not guaranteed to be semantically unrelated.

The broad claim that CFM enables explanations for “any” or “all” downstream vision tasks is overstated. Only three task families are demonstrated, and caption steering is supported mainly by qualitative examples without quantitative intervention-success, specificity, or side-effect measurements. Captioning also consumes reconstructed dense tokens, so stronger faithfulness evidence connecting named concepts to generated text would be valuable.

The method is largely a thoughtful integration of existing CLIP-DINOiser, Matryoshka SAE, BatchTopK, and concept-matching ideas, making the incremental novelty moderate despite the strong overall system contribution. Reproducibility is also weakened by the blank code link and by reliance on large-scale CC12M training and several empirically or qualitatively selected hyperparameters. Finally, Eqs. (3) and (4) use argmin over cosine similarity whereas Appendix Eq. (B.9) correctly uses argmax; this appears to be a readily correctable notation error rather than a substantive flaw.
